Title: A hybrid framework for heart disease prediction using classical and quantum-inspired machine learning techniques
Author: Ankur Kumar; Sanjay Dhanka; Abhinav Sharma; Rohit Bansal; Mochammad Fahlevi; Fazla Rabby; Mohammed Aljuaid
Abstract: This research proposes a hybrid framework integrating classical and quantum-inspired machine learning techniques to enhance heart disease prediction. Using a combined UCI dataset (Cleveland, Hungarian, Switzerland, Long Beach, Statlog) and preprocessing/feature selection, the study trains and optimizes both classical and quantum-inspired SVM-based models and evaluates them with 10-fold cross-validation and diagnostic metrics.
Method Used: Classical pipeline: Classical Genetic Algorithm (CGA) for feature selection + Classical Particle Swarm Optimization (CPSO) for SVM hyperparameter tuning + Classical SVM (CSVM). Quantum-inspired pipeline (simulated): Quantum Genetic Algorithm (QGA) for feature selection + Quantum Particle Swarm Optimization (QPSO) for hyperparameter tuning + Quantum SVM (QSVM) using Qiskit Aer simulator feature map/variational circuits.
Result: Combined dataset after deduplication: 918 samples (train/test 80/20). Classical model (CGA-CPSO-CSVM): accuracy 94.02% (TP 92, TN 81, FP 7, FN 4), sensitivity 95.83%, specificity 92.05%, F1 94.36%, AUC test 93%. Quantum-inspired model (QGA-QPSO-QSVM): accuracy 97.83% (TP 95, TN 85, FP 3, FN 1), sensitivity 98.96%, specificity 96.59%, F1 97.94%, average AUC 97%; LR+ 29.03 vs 12.05; LR- 0.01 vs 0.05; DOR 2691.67 vs 266.14. Runtime: 413.57 s (quantum-inspired) vs 362.92 s (classical). Feature reduction: 7/11 (37%) vs 9/11 (19%).
Conclusion: Quantum-inspired hybrid (QGA-QPSO-QSVM) outperformed classical hybrid across metrics while using fewer features, indicating potential for more accurate and interpretable heart disease prediction; however it incurs higher computational cost and is currently demonstrated via classical simulation rather than deployed quantum hardware.
Limitations: Quantum methods executed on classical simulators (not real QPU); increased runtime/overhead vs classical; external validation on larger/diverse real-world datasets not demonstrated; practical deployment constraints (hardware noise/coherence) remain for real quantum systems; interpretability and clinical integration need further work.

Title: A primer for quantum computing and its applications to healthcare and biomedical research
Author: Thomas J.S. Durant; Elizabeth Knight; Brent Nelson; Sarah Dudgeon; Seung J. Lee; Dominic Walliman; Hobart P. Young; Lucila Ohno-Machado; Wade L. Schulz
Abstract: Introduces quantum computing technologies for biomedical research and highlights future applications in healthcare, focusing on capabilities, benefits, limitations, and current state of hardware/software.
Method Used: Narrative literature review / primer (conceptual overview of quantum computing principles, algorithms, and biomedical application areas; no original experimental model).
Result: Summarizes that current quantum hardware is limited (noise, coherence, scalability, error correction) and many biomedical applications remain proof-of-concept or small-scale; QPUs should be viewed as accelerators complementary to CPUs/GPUs; practical quantum advantage for real-world biomedical tasks remains limited but research and access are expanding.
Conclusion: Quantum computing has promising potential for certain high-complexity biomedical problems, but real-world advantages are not yet broadly demonstrated; progress depends on hardware maturity, better software/tools, clearer benchmarking, and interdisciplinary collaboration.
Limitations: Not a primary experimental study; conclusions depend on available literature; limited actionable empirical performance comparisons; many cited applications are constrained by current device scale/noise and may not generalize to full-sized real-world datasets.

Title: A Quantum-Enhanced Precision Medicine Application to Support Data-Driven Clinical Decisions for the Personalized Treatment of Advanced Knee Osteoarthritis
Author: Nima Heidari; Stefano Olgiati; Davide Meloni; Mark Slevin; Ali Noorani; Federico Pirovano; Leonard Azamfirei
Abstract: Quantum computing and quantum machine learning (QML) are promising experimental technologies that can improve precision medicine applications by reducing computational complexity of algorithms driven by big, unstructured, real-world data.
Method Used: Quantum neural network (QNN) classifier (parameterized quantum circuit; Qiskit OpflowQNN) trained on clinicodemographic features (age, preoperative Oxford Knee Score, Kellgren-Lawrence grade); COBYLA optimizer; Aer simulator with 1024 shots; train/test split (113/57).
Result: Test set (n=57; 34 responders, 23 non-responders): correctly classified 28/34 responders and 6/23 non-responders; sensitivity 0.8235; specificity 0.2609; F1 0.7088; LR+ 1.1142; LR- 0.6765; DOR 2.0.
Conclusion: Preliminary validation suggests QML-based decision support for personalized treatment selection in advanced knee osteoarthritis is promising, but performance (especially specificity) is limited and requires larger real-world datasets and clinical validation.
Limitations: Small validation dataset; low specificity/high false positives; outliers handling may affect generalizability; external validation required; limited features and only one treatment modality.

Title: A quantum-optimized approach for breast cancer detection using SqueezeNet-SVM
Author: Anas Bilal; Ali Alkhathlan; Faris A. Kateb; Alishba Tahir; Muhammad Shafiq; Haixia Long
Abstract: Breast cancer is one of the most aggressive types of cancer, and its early diagnosis is crucial for reducing mortality rates and ensuring timely treatment.
Method Used: Hybrid CAD pipeline: mammogram preprocessing + SqueezeNet feature extraction; SVM classifier with hyperparameters optimized via quantum-inspired binary Grey Wolf Optimizer (Q-BGWO); evaluated via 5/10/15-fold cross-validation on MIAS, INbreast, DDSM, CBIS-DDSM.
Result: Reported best: on CBIS-DDSM with 15-fold CV: accuracy=0.99 (99%), sensitivity=0.98 (98%), specificity=1.00 (100%).
Conclusion: Q-BGWO-SQSVM achieves near state-of-the-art / benchmark-leading mammography classification and is presented as a reliable, efficient approach for early breast cancer detection, with further validation recommended.
Limitations: Reliance on benchmark datasets and cross-validation; clinical real-world deployment not validated; performance depends on preprocessing/augmentation/ROI selection.

Title: A systematic review of quantum machine learning for digital health
Author: Riddhi S. Gupta; Carolyn E. Wood; Teyl Engstrom; Jason D. Pole; Sally Shrapnel
Abstract: This systematic review assesses whether quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms outperform existing classical methods for clinical decisioning or health service delivery.
Method Used: Systematic review (PRISMA; SPICE framework; PROSPERO registered) of QML in digital health; searched PubMed/Embase/IEEE/Scopus/arXiv (2015-01-01 to 2024-10-06); screened 4915 records to 169 eligible.
Result: Key synthesis: no consistent empirical performance advantage of QML over classical methods in digital health; most studies rely on ideal simulations; limited scaling, limited uncertainty reporting, and inadequate noise characterization; only 16 studies used realistic operating conditions.
Conclusion: Current evidence base is insufficient to claim empirical quantum utility in digital health; future work should establish scalability, uncertainty, noise robustness, and stronger benchmarking vs classical methods under realistic conditions.
Limitations: Many studies excluded for low technical rigor; most evidence not on realistic hardware/noise; heterogeneous metrics impede meta-analysis.
